transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-03-11
Time: 16:00 UTC
Duration: ~42 minutes
Attendees: Eva Martinez (Redwood AE), Samir Patel (Redwood SE), Maya Chen (CTO, Orion), Arjun Rao (Lead Engineer, Orion), Priya Singh (PM, Orion)

Auto-summary (auto-generated, may be imperfect): Discussed SDK integration details for function/tool calling, structured output schema validation, and next steps for benchmarks. Some audio dropouts; speaker attribution automated.

Topics: SDK usage, function/tool calls, structured output JSON, latency/cost, security docs, benchmarks

[00:00] Eva Martinez: Hey everyone good to see you, thanks for joining the weekly POC sync. Quick roll call — Eva from Redwood, Samir our SE, and then Orion team?
[00:08] Maya Chen: Hi it's Maya here.
[00:10] Arjun Rao: Arjun.
[00:11] Priya Singh: Priya here.
[00:13] Samir Patel: Samir on the Redwood side, thanks folks.
[00:16] Eva: Ok goal today is to go over the integration progress, the results you ran last week against the SDK instrumented app, then dive into the structured output and function-calling behaviour. Roughly 30 minutes for updates and 10-12 for action items and next steps.

[00:45] Maya: Quick note, last week we ran the sample prompts through staging and saw some schema drift on the JSON output, a few missing fields and occasionally an extra nested array where our parser choked.
[00:53] Arjun: Right, and latency was kinda spiky at peak — not sure if that's the SDK client side batching settings or the endpoint config.

[01:12] Samir: Thanks, that's useful. On the schema drift, did you use the function-call (tool) mode or just plain generation with a post-parse step?
[01:20] Arjun: We used the function-call mode in the SDK for the majority, but for a small subset the app still calls the model directly and then runs internal validation.

[01:28] Samir: OK that helps. Two places to focus: 1) structured output enforcement in the model call (we can use function definitions with strict JSON schema in the call) and 2) client-side validation as a fallback. The SDK supports specifying a JSON schema for the function response so the runtime returns consistent shapes, though sometimes the model will still hallucinate or put values slightly off type.

[01:52] Eva: Also worth calling out KV cache/prefix caching — if you have repeated prompts we saw drift when caching token prefixes across different conversation contexts. You might need to flush or namespace the cache per user/session.

[02:10] Priya: Can you explain a bit more about the JSON schema enforcement and how strict it is? Will Redwood reject a response that doesn't match?

[02:18] Samir: Good question. The SDK has a validate step that will attempt to coerce or reject based on the schema you pass. There are three behaviors: best-effort coerce (tries to convert types), strict reject (runtime returns an error and you get an error code to handle), or sanitized fallback (returns best-effort output plus a validation flag). We recommend strict for critical fields and best-effort for non-blocking metadata.

[02:44] Arjun: That strict reject — does that add latency or extra calls?

[02:48] Samir: Minimal. It's done inline in the runtime, so you get a validation result as part of the response. If it rejects, it's a single response with an error code; the overhead is a few ms. The bigger latency source is streaming vs non-streaming and your batch size.

[03:05] Maya: About streaming, we saw quicker time-to-first-token when streaming enabled but then our client had to buffer and reassemble function payloads. Any recommended patterns?

[03:14] Samir: Pattern we see: stream the tokens to reduce TTFB, but for function/tool calls buffer until an end-of-function marker then run schema validation. SDK has helpers to reassemble streamed function responses into a validated JSON blob. We'll share sample code.

[03:32] Eva: Let's talk about the spiky latency Arjun mentioned. Do you have your client batching enabled? What batch size did you set?

[03:38] Arjun: We left it at default — which I think the SDK set to 8 concurrent requests and a max batch of 4.

[03:45] Samir: Defaults are conservative. For low-latency interactive apps, drop batch size to 1-2 and smaller concurrency, or enable prefetching with a hot pool. For throughput, larger batch sizes are cheaper per token. If you need consistent p95, Dedicated helps because you get reserved GPU pools.

[04:05] Maya: We're evaluating dedicated vs hosted for pilot. Security folks want VPC and KMS. What's the lift to run in Private?

[04:12] Eva: For Private we provide a customer-managed control plane and KMS integration — it takes some infra work on your side: network peering, firewall rules, and certs. We have an on-prem package too if you need air-gapped. We'll send the security pack.

[04:28] Priya: Related — we got a question from security: does Redwood retain prompts or transcript logs by default? We need a clear retention setting to comply with our policies.

[04:36] Eva: By default for hosted there is 30-day retention but you can opt-out; Dedicated/Private can be configured to retain none and ship logs to your SIEM. We'll include the SOC 2 and retention options in the security doc.

[04:48] Arjun: Back to structured output: when the model returns an extra unexpected field we prefer it to be ignored rather than breaking our parser. Can SDK strip unknown fields automatically?

[04:55] Samir: Yes — the validation options include 'stripUnknown' which will remove unknown keys. That's commonly used when schema needs to be strict for required keys but tolerant for extras.

[05:08] Maya: Any recommendations around idempotency for function/tool invocations? We have downstream side effects and must avoid duplicate actions.

[05:15] Samir: Two patterns: 1) client side generate idempotency keys per logical request and pass into function metadata; 2) have the function itself be idempotent by checking a request store. Redwood also surfaces request ids in traces so you can reconcile. We'll include an example pattern in the playbook.

[05:34] Priya: On cost — if we switch from hosted to dedicated, how quickly do we see per-token cost improvements?

[05:40] Eva: Depends on utilization. At 60-70% utilization across committed GPUs you typically see 30-50% lower per-token compared to on-demand hosted, given batching and reserved capacity. Our Optimize tool will run recommendations once you upload usage profile.

[05:58] Arjun: For the benchmark you requested, we have three traffic shapes: steady low throughput, bursty peak, and conversational multi-turn. We'll share the traces.

[06:06] Samir: Perfect — for the benchmark we'll run p50/p95/p99 latency and cost per 1k tokens across hosted and a dedicated equivalent. Also we'll test structured output failure modes (invalid JSON, truncated streams).

[06:20] Eva: Quick demo snippet idea — Samir do you want to walk through the streaming function call example you pushed to the sandbox repo?

[06:27] Samir: Sure. I'm going to summarize — code in the repo sets up a function definition with a JSON schema for the response and calls client.streamFunctionCall(...). The client yields token events; once we see the function_end event we reassemble and call validate(schema). The repo includes a helper to auto-retry with backoff on validation reject. Note: the naming in the transcript might say 'Redwood Console' but the repo is under 'redwood-infer-playbook' — minor mismatch folks, sorry AI captioning in the meeting tool sometimes mangles names.

[07:00] Arjun: That repo link would be great. Also any example in our language (Go + Node) please.

[07:06] Samir: Yep Node and Go are in the repo; will send link.

[07:12] Maya: We had one case where the function call returned valid JSON but numbers were strings — type coercion bit us. Should we coerce server-side?

[07:19] Samir: I'd recommend strict typing for critical numeric fields; for non-critical numeric metadata you can coerce with fallback. We'll provide a recommended field-level policy for your schema.

[07:35] Priya: Anything else on instrumentation/tracing? Our SREs want to correlate Redwood request ids with our logs.

[07:42] Eva: We add request_id headers and the Console exposes per-request traces; you can export traces to your Datadog/CloudWatch. We'll include the tracing hooks doc.

[07:52] Maya: Cool. On timeline — assuming benchmark looks good, we want to canary structured output in staging in two weeks and then expand. That sound right?

[07:59] Eva: Totally reasonable. We'll be available to support canary rollout.

[08:05] Arjun: A couple of small bugs we noticed in SDK v0.9.1: one edge case when stream disconnects mid-function the reassembly helper throws a null pointer. Any workaround?

[08:14] Samir: We're tracking that as ticket RW-5478. Workaround is to guard the reassembly step and if you detect mid-function disconnect, call client.resumeStream or fallback to non-streaming fetch. Patch for v0.9.2 goes out this week.

[08:28] Priya: Good. Anything from your side Eva?

[08:32] Eva: Just to recap next steps and owners — we'll share the repo, code snippets, security pack, and updated pricing. Samir will own the SDK snippets and patch info. Arjun to share traces. Maya to confirm infra deep dive attendees.

[08:48] Maya: One question — any competitive notes? Our infra team asked how Redwood compares to Anthropic in terms of function-calling stability.

[08:55] Samir: High-level: stability is similar but our differentiator is server-side JSON schema enforcement and integrated KV/prefix caching controls, plus the Dedicated reserved pools for predictable p95. We'll send a short doc comparing features.

[09:10] Eva: Ok let's capture action items.
